author: Origen of Alexandria
occasion: Brief explanatory notes on difficult phrases in the Greek text of Judges, clarifying wording and the theological reasons behind events.
argument: Origen notes an alternative reading of Judges 15:19: instead of 'God broke the wound in the jawbone,' the text means 'He split the earth by the blow of the jawbone, and waters came out.' He then asks why the Israelites were defeated despite justly going out against Benjamin, and explains that because of earlier causes, after being defeated once and then a second time, wrath came upon the wrongdoers, and the Israelites won a just judgment. Origen praises the Israelites for not thinking anything evil against God, but rather not ceasing to weep until they obtained justice against the wrongdoers. He also sees the prophecy 'Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he devours, and in the evening he distributes food' fulfilled here: for having conquered first, Benjamin became food for the people at the last.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Origen notes an alternative reading of Judges 15:19: instead of 'God broke the wound in the jawbone,' the text means 'He split the earth by the blow of the jawbone, and waters came out.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Στίχ. ιθ΄. Καὶ ἔῤῥηξεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ τραῦμα τὸ ἐν σιαγόνι, καὶ ἐξῆλθεν ἐξ αὐτοῦ ὕδωρ. Ἀντὶ τοῦ· Ἔῤῥηξε τῇ πληγῇ τῆς σιαγόνος τὴν γῆν, καὶ ἐξῆλθεν ὕδατα.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Origen notes that 'God broke the wound in the jawbone, and water came out from it' is read 'instead of' (ἀντὶ τοῦ) 'He broke the earth by the blow of the jawbone, and waters came out.' The brief reverses the relationship: the 'earth' reading is the alternative, not the main text.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He then asks why the Israelites were defeated despite justly going out against Benjamin, and explains that because of earlier causes, after being defeated once and then a second time, wrath came upon the wrongdoers, and the Israelites won a just judgment.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τίνος ἕνεκεν ἡττῶνται δικαίως ἐπεξελθόντες; Ἢ δηλονότι διὰ προλαβούσας αἰτίας. Καὶ ὁ ψαλμός φησιν· Ὅταν λάβω καιρὸν, ἐγὼ εὐθύτητας κρινῶ. Εἶτα dicit : μετὰ τὸ ἡττηθῆναι καὶ μίαν καὶ δευτέραν, μετῆλθεν ἡ ὀργὴ ἐπὶ τοὺς ἠδικηκότας, νικῶσι δικαίαν δίκην
_unresolved_facts.fix: Origen asks why the Israelites were defeated despite justly going out against Benjamin, and explains that it was because of earlier causes. Then, after being defeated once and then a second time, wrath came upon the wrongdoers, and the Israelites won a just judgment. The 'earlier causes' (προλαβούσας αἰτίας) explain the initial defeats, not the eventual victory; the brief conflates the timeline.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He also sees the prophecy 'Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he devours, and in the evening he distributes food' fulfilled here: for having conquered first, Benjamin became food for the people at the last.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τό Βενιαμὶν λύκος ἅρπαξ· πραῒ ἔδεται, καὶ τὸ ἑ. (76) διαδώσει τροφὴν, ἐνταῦθα πληροῦται. Καὶ γὰρ πρότερον νικήσας, ἔσχατον βρῶμα τοῦ λαοῦ γέγονε.
_unresolved_facts.fix: He sees the prophecy 'Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he devours, and in the evening he will distribute food' fulfilled here: for having conquered first, he became food for the people at the last. The brief misattributes the prophecy fulfillment: it is the tribe of Benjamin that is the wolf, not 'Benjamin's fate' as an abstract; and the prophecy says 'he will distribute food' (διαδώσει), not that Benjamin 'became food'—rather, Benjamin became food (βρῶμα) for the people, which inverts the expected meaning of 'distributes food.'
